query: For high-entropy-alloy coatings used in wear-resistant applications, what single intervention could improve wear resistance across operating temperatures? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise identical unmodified coating, the temperature and sliding conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of titanium (Ti) into an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coating will improve wear resistance across a wide operating temperature range (room temperature to 900°C) by promoting the formation of a stable, protective oxide layer at elevated temperatures while maintaining a fine-grained, multiphase microstructure that resists abrasive wear at lower temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coating with equimolar composition of Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni, prepared via laser cladding or sputtering on a steel substrate, exhibiting a single-phase FCC structure with moderate hardness and wear resistance at room temperature but degraded performance at elevated temperatures due to softening and lack of protective oxide formation.
generation.intervention: Addition of 0.5 mole fraction of titanium (Ti) to the base AlCoCrFeNi composition, resulting in an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 coating.
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures from room temperature (25°C) to 900°C, under reciprocating sliding wear conditions with a load of 10 N and a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s in an atmospheric environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase microstructure consisting of two finely distributed body-centered cubic (BCC) phases and a complex intermetallic phase, along with the in-situ generation of a protective Cr2O3/Al2O3-rich oxide layer at elevated temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the Ti addition promotes the formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and wear. Simultaneously, the multiphase microstructure provides enhanced hardness and resistance to plastic deformation at lower temperatures, preventing wear degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 coating will exhibit a 30-50% reduction in wear rate compared to the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi coating across the entire temperature range, with a slight decrease in the coefficient of friction at temperatures above 500°C due to the protective oxide layer.
generation.baseline: Unmodified AlCoCrFeNi coating with equimolar composition, exhibiting moderate wear resistance at room temperature but significant degradation at temperatures above 500°C due to softening and lack of protective oxide formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for coatings with Ti content between 0.3 and 0.7 mole fraction; beyond this range, excessive Ti may lead to brittle phase formation and reduced wear resistance. The effect is limited to atmospheric environments where oxide formation is possible.
generation.uncertainty: The exact Ti content required for optimal performance may vary depending on the specific processing method (e.g., laser cladding vs. sputtering) and substrate material. Additionally, the long-term stability of the oxide layer under cyclic thermal loading is not fully characterized.
generation.falsification_experiment: Prepare AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 and AlCoCrFeNi coatings using the same processing method. Conduct reciprocating wear tests at 25°C, 500°C, and 900°C under identical conditions (10 N load, 0.1 m/s sliding speed). If the AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 coating shows no improvement in wear rate (or worse performance) at any of these temperatures compared to the unmodified coating, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
